Significance, Power, Sample Size and Peeking

What separates a team that computes a sample size from a team that knows what its evidence is worth.

The working version of this topic ends with a sensible instruction: decide the sample size in advance, do not stop early, beware novelty. All of it is true and almost none of it survives contact with a real experimentation programme. Traffic is clustered. Metrics are ratios with heavy tails. Most users never see the feature. The judge scoring the outcome is itself a model. And the organisation cannot wait three weeks for every decision. What follows is where the arithmetic comes from, what it assumes, what expert teams substitute when the assumptions fail, and where competent people still disagree.

1. Two decisions, two weeks apart

On Tuesday, 3 March 2026, Ira Kanungo, Director of Product at Chausar Freight Exchange in Pune, had a ten-day-old experiment and a board meeting on 12 March. Chausar matches full-truckload shippers with fleet owners across thirty-four intercity lanes; its new auto-bid tool, which submits a fleet owner's standing price on matching loads without a manual tap, had been switched on for seventeen lanes and left off for the other seventeen. Across those lanes 41,200 shipments had been posted in treatment and 39,900 in control; booking-within-one-hour ran at 46.8% against 44.1%, and the dashboard reported p = 0.011.

The question that number answered was the wrong question. Chausar had randomised lanes, not shipments. Shipments on the same lane share a shipper base, a seasonal pattern and often a single large customer; treating 41,200 correlated shipments as 41,200 independent observations is the statistical equivalent of counting a busload of colleagues as an opinion poll. Ira's analyst, Vibhuti Rane, had flagged it on day two. The honest analysis had seventeen observations per arm, not forty-one thousand, and Ira had nine days to work out whether seventeen was enough to commit ₹1.8 crore of platform incentives.

Eight days later, on 11 March, Tanmay Raichur, Group Product Manager at Sanyog Intelligence in Hyderabad, faced a different shape of the same problem. Sanyog sells an AI support copilot to 140 enterprise tenants — banks, insurers, two airlines — and was evaluating a model upgrade on containment rate: the share of conversations resolved without escalation to a human agent. The upgrade scored 40.3% against a 38.1% baseline across 84,000 conversations, p = 0.0004. But no human had read those conversations; containment was labelled by a grader model whose agreement with human reviewers, audited the previous quarter, sat at roughly 92% in each direction. The upgrade also cost 2.3× per conversation in inference — ₹94 lakh a year at Sanyog's volume. Tanmay needed to know not whether the difference was real, but how much of a real difference the measurement could be hiding, and whether 140 tenants of wildly unequal size could carry the claim at all.

2. The idea, and the four schools that split over it

Stated precisely: this machinery converts a business tolerance for two kinds of mistake into a quantity of evidence that must be gathered before a decision is taken, and peeking is any practice that consumes that evidence more than once without paying for the extra look. Alpha is the probability of acting on a difference that does not exist; power (1 − β) the probability of noticing one that does; sample size is what the two, plus the metric's variance and the minimum detectable effect, jointly imply.

The history is a sequence of borrowings from fields with higher stakes. Ronald Fisher's Statistical Methods for Research Workers (1925) gave the p-value as a continuous measure of evidence against a null, with no alternative hypothesis and therefore no power. Neyman and Pearson, between 1928 and 1933, replaced evidence with decision: fix α and β in advance, derive n, act, and accept a known long-run error rate as the price. Abraham Wald's sequential probability ratio test, developed for wartime munitions inspection and published in 1945, established that a correctly designed test may look continuously and stop early, sampling only until the evidence crosses a boundary calibrated for repeated looks. Armitage, McPherson and Rowe quantified the damage from uncalibrated looking in 1969; Pocock (1977) and O'Brien and Fleming (1979) gave clinical trials usable group-sequential boundaries, and Lan and DeMets (1983) generalised these into alpha-spending functions. Technology firms rediscovered all of it between 2007 and 2017, adding variance reduction from pre-experiment covariates and the always-valid p-values that let a growth dashboard be refreshed hourly without lying.

Four positions now coexist in mature programmes, and they are not interchangeable.

Table 1. What each school will and will not sign. Most disputes inside a company are between people who have silently adopted different rows.
SchoolWill signWill not sign
Fisherianp grades evidence against the null on a continuum; 0.049 and 0.051 are the same observation.That 0.05 is a decision rule, or that "not significant" licenses a claim of no effect.
Neyman–PearsonFix α, β and n before the data; look once; accept the error rates as the cost of a repeatable process.That p is the probability the hypothesis is true, or that a test may be extended after seeing the result.
Sequential / always-validContinuous monitoring is legitimate when the boundary is designed for it; pre-commitment moves from n to the stopping rule.That fixed-horizon p-values may be read early "with judgement", or that sequential methods carry no sample-size tax.

Bayesian practice cuts across these rather than sitting beside them: it reports the posterior probability that treatment beats control and the expected loss from shipping, and is genuinely less troubled by optional stopping at the level of the posterior. It is not immune to the underlying problem, because a stopping rule tuned to the posterior still changes how often the organisation ships things that do not work — the quantity a VP of Product actually cares about.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Start with the cost of looking. A fixed-horizon test read once at α = 0.05 has a 5% false-positive rate by construction. Read at k equally spaced interim points and stopped the first time p dips below 0.05, its true rate climbs steeply: 8.3% for two looks, 10.7% for three, 14.2% for five, 19.3% for ten, 24.6% for twenty. A daily dashboard on a three-week test is twenty looks. One experiment in four is then a false alarm, and nobody in the room can tell which.

The fix is not to stop looking but to spend alpha deliberately. A group-sequential design divides the total 5% across planned interim analyses, requiring a stricter nominal p early — when little information has accumulated — and relaxing towards the end. Pocock's boundary is constant across looks (about 0.0158 for five), making early stopping easy at the cost of a strict final threshold. O'Brien–Fleming spends almost nothing early, running roughly 0.00001, 0.0013, 0.0084, 0.0225 and 0.0413 across five looks, so a test that goes the distance is judged at nearly the usual bar. Always-valid methods — mixture sequential probability ratio tests and confidence sequences — extend this to continuous monitoring, at a price: against a true effect equal to the MDE, expect to run 20–60% longer than a fixed-horizon design; against an effect two or three times the MDE, you often stop in half the time.

Now the sample size itself, and the two corrections that matter more than the formula. For a proportion metric the standard expression is

n per arm = (Zα/2 + Zβ)² × [p₁(1−p₁) + p₂(1−p₂)] / (p₂ − p₁)²

Applied to Sanyog's upgrade with p₁ = 0.381, a 2-point MDE (p₂ = 0.401), α = 0.05 two-sided and 80% power: the bracket is 7.84, the variances sum to 0.4760, the denominator is 0.0004, and n ≈ 9,330 conversations per arm — trivially available. Two corrections then destroy that comfort.

The first is measurement attenuation. Because the grader mislabels roughly 8% of conversations in each direction, a true 2.0-point difference is observed as 2.0 × (1 − 0.08 − 0.08) = 1.68 points. Required sample scales with the inverse square of the observed effect: (2.0 / 1.68)² = 1.42, so Sanyog needs about 13,250 per arm to retain 80% power against the same true effect. Worse, if grader error is differential — if the newer model writes in a register the grader rewards — attenuation becomes bias, which no sample size cures.

The second is clustering. Sanyog assigns tenants, not conversations; Chausar assigns lanes, not shipments. The design effect is

DEFF = 1 + (m − 1) × ICC   →   effective n = nominal n / DEFF

where m is the average cluster size and ICC the intra-cluster correlation. Chausar's lanes average 1,212 shipments with an ICC of 0.02 — modest, and typical of behavioural metrics — so DEFF = 1 + 1,211 × 0.02 = 25.2, and 41,200 shipments are worth about 1,635 independent observations. Sanyog's tenants average 600 conversations at an ICC of 0.05: DEFF = 31.0, reducing 84,000 conversations to roughly 2,710. Both reported p-values were wrong by more than an order of magnitude in the denominator.

Two further moves belong in the expert's standard sequence. Triggered analysis restricts both arms to users who actually reached the changed surface: if only 22% of Chausar's fleet owners ever open the bid screen, an effect measured on all of them is diluted by roughly 0.22, and the MDE must be stated on the triggered population or the test is under-designed four- or fivefold. Variance reduction — regression adjustment on pre-period behaviour, known in industry as CUPED — multiplies the metric's variance by (1 − ρ²). Chausar's lanes are stable week to week: ρ = 0.72 gives a multiplier of 0.48, worth more than doubling the number of lanes and costing nothing but analysis. For clustered designs it is usually the highest-return technique available, because adding clusters means adding cities.

4. When the machinery applies, and when it misleads

Four conditions can be stated as testable claims. (a) Units are independent conditional on assignment. Chausar fails at the shipment level, passes at the lane level; Sanyog fails at the conversation level and passes, weakly, at the tenant level. (b) There is no interference between arms. Chausar fails this too: a fleet owner in a treated lane who wins more loads has less capacity for an adjacent control lane, so part of the "lift" is capacity moved rather than created — which is why marketplaces switch to switchback or region-level designs. (c) The effect is stable over the window. Both fail in week one, Chausar from fleet-owner learning, Sanyog from tenants adjusting escalation rules once they notice the change. (d) The metric is measured without differential error. Chausar passes; Sanyog's model-graded metric is exactly where this is in doubt.

The machinery becomes actively misleading in three situations. When the decision is irreversible and asymmetric — a pricing change with contractual consequences, a regulated disclosure — controlling a 5% false-positive rate is the wrong objective; expected loss is. When the population is small, as in most B2B feature work, an honest power calculation returns "impossible" and a team that insists on significance simply stops learning. And when the treatment changes the composition of the population rather than the behaviour of a fixed one, the difference in means is a valid comparison of two worlds but not an estimate of what the feature does to anybody.

5. Hard edges, and what mature companies really do

In multi-product companies the seam is metric ownership. A recommendation change that lifts a ten-minute-delivery product's conversion may depress the pharmacy product's basket size; if the two report to different VPs, the experiment is scored on the metric of whoever ran it. Mature programmes answer with a pre-registered guardrail set — a fixed list of cross-product metrics every experiment reports whether or not they help — and a non-inferiority rule: ship unless a guardrail's interval crosses a stated harm threshold, which is deliberately a different test from "is it significant".

Two-sided platforms cannot randomise users without contaminating the market. The honest designs are switchbacks (alternating treatment and control across time windows in one city, analysed at the window level) and city- or region-level clusters, both of which reduce effective n to the dozens. Regulated products — a lending flow under RBI rules, a diagnostic under CDSCO — add a constraint: the treatment arm must satisfy the same obligations as control, so the experiment usually tests presentation rather than substance, and "no significant difference" may be the desired outcome rather than a failure. Hardware-plus-software adds the firmware release cycle, where the assignment unit is a device that cannot be re-randomised, cohorts are confounded with manufacturing batch, and the interesting effects appear months later.

AI-native products bring a distinct set: outputs are stochastic, so the same user in the same arm gets different experiences; the primary metric is often a preference judgement produced by another model; and the treatment can degrade a small segment badly while lifting the average, because model behaviour is not smooth across input types. Serious AI teams run paired designs (both models on the same input, order randomised), report segment-level intervals as a matter of course, and audit the grader against human labels every cycle, treating grader drift as a data-quality incident.

What mature companies say is that every launch is gated on a well-powered experiment. What they do is maintain three tiers: a small set of high-stakes decisions run to a pre-registered fixed horizon; a large middle tier monitored with always-valid boundaries and shipped on the boundary; and a long tail shipped on guardrails alone with no power to detect anything, explicitly logged as unmeasured. The tiering is the mature part; pretending the third tier does not exist is not.

6. Eight nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Variance is a lever; traffic usually is not. The tell is a team whose first response to an underpowered test is to request more traffic or a longer window. An expert attacks the metric's variance instead: trigger-restrict the population, winsorise a heavy-tailed revenue metric at the 99th percentile, switch to a bounded conversion indicator, apply pre-period adjustment. Each can halve the required sample in an afternoon. The obvious reading — that sample size is the binding constraint — is wrong because sample size enters the formula only as a divisor of variance, and variance is the term you control.

Power is a property of a metric, not of an experiment. When someone says a test is "powered at 80%", the expert asks: for which metric, at what effect size? A test comfortably powered for conversion is typically powered only for a 30% change in revenue-per-user and for nothing on retention. So guardrails are almost always underpowered, and "no significant harm" routinely means "we could not have seen harm of the size we should worry about".

A significant estimate from an underpowered test is systematically too large. This is the winner's curse, or Type M error: conditional on clearing the bar, a low-powered test can only have cleared it by landing in the upper tail, so the published effect exaggerates the truth. The tell is a portfolio of shipped wins whose claimed contributions sum to far more than the company metric actually moved — a gap most organisations attribute to "execution" rather than to the arithmetic that guaranteed it.

Peeking at the design is the same offence as peeking at the p-value. Extending a test by a week, adding a segment after seeing the totals, swapping the primary metric, excluding a "contaminated" cohort — each is a decision made downstream of the data, and each spends error rate as an extra look does. The tell is a results document whose analysis plan is richer than the launch document. The obvious reading — that this is careful analysis, not cheating — is wrong because the forking happens conditional on what was seen, which is the definition of the problem.

A null result is an interval, not a verdict. The expert reads "no significant difference" by asking whether the confidence interval excludes the effect worth shipping. An interval of [−1.2%, +4.0%] against a 2% MDE is not evidence of no effect; it is an experiment that failed to answer its own question. The tell is a summary reporting a p-value without an interval — usually a sign the interval would have been embarrassing.

Sample ratio mismatch voids the whole analysis, and small imbalances are the dangerous ones. A 50/50 split delivering 20,131 and 19,504 users looks close; the chi-square statistic is 9.9, p ≈ 0.0016, and the split is broken. Because SRM almost always originates in assignment, logging or a treatment-side crash, the missing users are not missing at random — they are disproportionately the ones the treatment failed. The tell is an analyst who checks the split before any outcome and refuses to discuss results until it passes.

Novelty and primacy are opposite-signed and both look like drift. Curious users inflate week one; habituated users resent change and depress it. Calendar-time plots confound both with weekday cycles and campaigns. The expert plots effect size by days-since-first-exposure, aligning cohorts on their own clocks, and treats monotone decay towards zero as a reason for a long-horizon holdback rather than as noise.

The threshold is a price, not a law. An expert sets α by what a false ship costs relative to a missed win. Chausar's auto-bid commits ₹1.8 crore and is hard to withdraw, so α = 0.01 and 90% power are defensible even at the cost of lanes and weeks; a reversible copy change may deserve α = 0.20 and fast iteration. The tell is a team that has never used a number other than 0.05 and cannot say why 0.05 fits their decision.

7. What actually differs across product types and stages

Consumer products at scale are the easy case and the usual source of bad advice: sample arrives quickly, so the binding constraint is discipline rather than arithmetic, and the industry's canonical guidance is written from here. B2B and enterprise invert every term — the unit is the account, n is in the hundreds, heterogeneity is enormous — so the honest response is to widen the MDE dramatically, use paired or stratified designs matching accounts on size, and supplement with structured qualitative evidence rather than pretending to significance. Platforms are constrained by interference, not by users: Chausar has plenty of shipments and almost no independent units. Hardware is constrained by the release cycle. AI products are constrained by outcome measurement, because the metric itself is an estimate.

Where the difference is claimed but not real: the statistics do not change by product type. The formulas, the error rates and the cost of peeking are identical everywhere. What changes is which term is scarce — units, variance, effect size or measurement quality — and therefore which lever to pull first. By stage, an early company with a few thousand weekly actives should run almost no significance tests and instead ship changes big enough not to need one, reserving measurement for guardrails; a scaled company has the opposite problem, a high volume of small real effects that need variance reduction and sequential methods to detect economically.

8. Three experiments, one of them a wreck

Chausar's redesign. Vibhuti Rane rebuilt the test at lane level: 34 lanes stratified into three volume tiers before randomisation to cut between-lane variance, CUPED adjustment on eight prior weeks of lane booking rate (ρ = 0.72, multiplier 0.48), MDE widened from 2 to 4 points because the design could not support less, and a cluster-level t-test on 17 versus 17 lane means. Six weeks later: +3.1 points, 95% interval [0.4, 5.8] — significant at 0.05, but with a lower bound below the 4-point MDE. The team reported it as "consistent with a worthwhile effect, not proof of one" and shipped with a permanent 10% lane holdback.

Sanyog's paired evaluation. Tanmay abandoned the tenant split and ran both models on the same 6,000 conversations, with 900 scored by human reviewers alongside the grader. Pairing removed between-conversation variance, the dominant term; the human subsample calibrated the grader's attenuation and, more usefully, showed the gain was concentrated in two tenants with unusually long conversations and slightly negative for the airlines. Overall containment gain survived at +1.4 points, below the 2-point threshold that justified ₹94 lakh of inference cost.

Kaudi Fresh, and what it cost. Kaudi Fresh, a Chennai grocery retailer, shipped a checkout redesign in 2025 on a day-nine peek at p = 0.032 in a test scoped for eighteen days, reporting a 6.4% conversion lift. Post-rollout conversion rose about 1.1%, within seasonal movement. A re-test against a 5% holdout put the true effect near 0.8% overall and roughly −3% on low-end Android devices, where the new checkout was slow. The recovery was structural rather than analytical: a permanent 5% holdout, removal of live p-values from the dashboard before the pre-registered date, and a reconciliation in which 23 previously shipped "wins" were re-examined and 11 failed to replicate. The reconciliation was the expensive part and the only part that changed behaviour, because it turned an abstract statistical argument into a number the CFO recognised.

9. Failure modes and their early warning signs

Table 3. The five failures that account for most wasted experimentation capacity, with the question that catches each one early and what it costs when it is caught late instead.

Two deserve emphasis because they are invisible rather than merely ignored. Dilution has a signature: a team whose qualitative research strongly suggests a change works, and whose experiments always come back flat. Usually the denominator includes users who never saw the surface. Grader drift is the newest and least-governed failure; the right response is to version the evaluation as code is versioned, and to refuse to compare effect sizes measured under different grader versions at all.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The first live dispute is whether always-valid inference should be the default. For: humans will look, and a method that assumes otherwise will be violated silently; confidence sequences make continuous monitoring honest and, for large effects, cheaper. Against: sequential methods impose a real width tax, they encourage stopping at the first crossing — which biases estimates upward exactly as peeking does — and they do not address the deeper problem, that teams stop when the answer is pleasing. The against case would be wrong if audits showed sequential-stopped experiments replicating as well as fixed-horizon ones; the published evidence is thin and mostly internal.

The second is whether significance testing should be abandoned for estimation. Its strongest form is not that p-values are invalid but that dichotomising a continuous measure of evidence destroys information the decision needs, that 0.05 bears no relation to any business loss function, and that the observable consequence — shipped effects that do not sum to the company's metric movement — is exactly what the theory predicts. The counter-argument is organisational, not statistical: a threshold is a commitment device that survives a VP with an OKR, and intervals invite negotiation in a way a pre-agreed rule does not. It would be wrong if teams using interval-based rules were shown to ship worse features; nobody has run that experiment on experimentation itself.

The third is how much of a roadmap should be gated on experiments at all. One camp holds that anything unmeasured is unmanaged and the discipline is worth its latency cost. The other holds that most product decisions concern effects too small or too slow for any feasible test, that gating them biases the roadmap towards the measurable — copy, colours, funnels — and away from the structural bets that differentiate a product, and that experimentation belongs as a guardrail against harm rather than as an arbiter of value. Both camps can point to companies that succeeded doing the opposite of what the other recommends, which is the honest state of the evidence.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in four visible ways. They spend effort before launch rather than after: the argument about MDE, randomisation unit and stopping rule happens in the design review, and the results meeting is short because nothing is left to decide. They speak in intervals and magnitudes rather than verdicts, as quick to say "this test could never have detected what we care about" as "this is significant". They ask about randomisation unit, triggered population and split check before the effect size is mentioned. And they keep a record of what was shipped, what was claimed and what the metric actually did, because the only real audit of an experimentation programme is whether its accumulated wins are visible in the company's numbers.

12. The decisions

Ira Kanungo went to the 12 March board meeting without a result. She presented the corrected analysis — seventeen lanes per arm, an effective sample near 1,600, a cluster-robust p of 0.19 — and asked for six more weeks and a stratified, CUPED-adjusted redesign, reasoning that a ₹1.8 crore commitment made on an analysis she knew to be wrong was worse than a delayed one. She also had the shipment-level p-value removed from every Chausar dashboard, because the wrong number was more dangerous than no number.

Tanmay Raichur recommended against the upgrade at full fleet: a +1.4-point gain concentrated in two tenants and slightly negative for two others did not justify ₹94 lakh a year. He proposed routing the upgraded model only to the long-conversation segment where the gain was real, and commissioned a quarterly human audit of the grader, on the view that Sanyog's binding constraint was not statistical power but the credibility of its ruler.

For discussion. (1) Chausar's corrected design supports an MDE of about 4.4 points, while the product team believes the true effect is nearer 2. What are Ira's options other than running longer, and what does each cost? (2) Sanyog's grader mislabels 8% of conversations each way. When is that benign, and what evidence would distinguish benign attenuation from bias favouring the newer model? (3) Kaudi Fresh found 11 of 23 shipped "wins" did not replicate. As its VP of Product, what would you change first — the statistics, the dashboard or the incentives — and what would the other two do in response?

13. Going deeper

  1. A/B testing fundamentals — randomisation units and guardrails, where most statistical errors originate.
  2. Descriptive statistics for PMs — variance, skew and standard error; without them, sample-size arithmetic is a black box you cannot argue with.
  3. When you can't A/B test — for B2B, marketplace and regulated cases where n is structurally too small; unlocks difference-in-differences, synthetic control, switchbacks.
  4. Experiment pitfalls — SRM, dilution, interference and instrumentation failures, each of which invalidates a correctly computed p-value.
  5. Bayesian vs frequentist interpretation — the expected-loss framing for asymmetric, irreversible decisions that 0.05 handles badly.
  6. Sequential testing and always-valid inference — the direct answer to peeking; unlocks continuous monitoring without Figure 1's error inflation.
  7. Heterogeneous treatment effects — the discipline behind Sanyog's segment finding; unlocks targeted rollouts and guards against average-positive, segment-harmful launches.
  8. Writing an experiment hypothesis — the pre-registration artefact that makes peeking detectable and stopping rules enforceable.
  9. Experimentation culture — whether the rules survive a quarter-end OKR; Kaudi Fresh's reconciliation was a cultural intervention, not a statistical one.
  10. Qual + quant feedback loop — the substitute when power is unattainable, and the early detector of dilution.
  11. Feature flags and flighting — the mechanism behind triggered analysis, holdbacks and staged ramps; a weak flagging layer caps experimental quality.
  12. Choosing experiment metrics — metric variance and sensitivity set the MDE before any calculation begins; the cheapest power you will ever buy.
  13. Experimentation platforms — where sequential boundaries, CUPED, SRM alarms and cluster-robust analysis become defaults rather than heroics.

Significance, Power, Sample Size — and the Temptation to Peek

Do I have enough users, and am I stopping too early?

It was 9:40 p.m. on Tuesday, 14 April 2026, and Meera Iyer, Senior Product Manager for Growth at Chakor Mart, a ten-minute grocery-delivery app headquartered in Bengaluru's Indiranagar, was refreshing an experiment dashboard for the fourth time that evening. Five days earlier, on 9 April, her team had shipped "One-Tap Reorder," a button on the order-confirmation screen letting a returning customer repeat their last basket without touching the search bar. Half of Chakor Mart's roughly 20,000 daily checkout sessions were being randomly assigned to see the button; the other half saw the old screen. That night, for the first time since launch, the dashboard's p-value for the primary metric — checkout conversion — had dipped to 0.041, just under the conventional 0.05 line the team used to call a result significant. Conversion in the treatment group stood at 4.38% against 4.02% in control, a lift of roughly 9%.

Her phone buzzed. Arvind Bhalla, VP of Growth, had seen the same number: "This is the OKR we needed. Can eng start the full rollout tomorrow?" Chakor Mart was seven weeks from closing a Series C round its CFO had pencilled in for Q3 2026, and a documented conversion win was the kind of slide investors liked. Building the button into every surface of the app, not just the confirmation screen, would cost roughly three sprints — about ₹40 lakh of loaded engineering time by Meera's estimate. Saying yes tonight, on five days of data instead of the sixteen her data scientist had scoped the test to run, was tempting and, as Meera was about to work out on a notepad, statistically indefensible.

The idea

At its core, this topic is a discipline for deciding, before looking at any data, how much data you need and exactly how you will judge it once it arrives — so that the judgment you eventually make is one you would trust from a stranger's experiment, not only your own hopeful one.

Four ideas sit inside that discipline. Statistical significance tests whether an observed difference between two groups is larger than random chance alone would typically produce, expressed as a p-value: the probability of seeing a difference at least this large if there were truly no effect. A p-value below a threshold chosen in advance, conventionally 0.05 (alpha, α), is the trigger a team agrees to treat as real. Statistical power is the probability that the test will detect a true effect of a given size if one genuinely exists, conventionally set at 80%; a low-power test can easily miss a real effect and report "no difference," not because nothing happened but because too few people were in the experiment to see it. Sample size is the number of users per arm the arithmetic requires, given the baseline rate, the smallest effect worth detecting — the minimum detectable effect, or MDE — and the chosen alpha and power. Peeking is checking results before that planned sample size is reached and making a stop-or-ship call on what the dashboard shows at that moment, which quietly multiplies the odds of a false alarm, as the arithmetic ahead will show.

The vocabulary is younger than most assume. Ronald Fisher, at England's Rothamsted research station, formalised the p-value and the 0.05 convention in his 1925 book Statistical Methods for Research Workers, to judge whether a fertiliser had changed a crop yield; his test had no formal concept of power. That came from Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson, whose 1928–1933 papers introduced two kinds of error — wrongly calling a non-effect real (Type I, governed by alpha) and wrongly calling a real effect noise (Type II, governed by beta, where power = 1 − β) — and with it the habit of fixing sample size before a test, not after. The sentence Meera could say without sounding glib: "We don't yet have enough evidence to tell a 9% lift apart from noise — and looking again tomorrow doesn't give us more evidence, it just gives us another chance to fool ourselves."

How it actually works

Running an experiment properly, in the order practitioners often skip, looks like this. First, name the hypothesis around one primary metric decided in advance — Meera's team had picked checkout conversion, not the seven secondary metrics also visible on the dashboard, so a good result elsewhere couldn't later be dressed up as the win. Second, establish the baseline: checkout conversion across the prior four weeks averaged 4.0%, with day-to-day variation the data team had already characterised. Third, decide the smallest lift worth the engineering cost of building the feature everywhere — the minimum detectable effect. This is a business judgment, not a statistical one: Meera and Arvind agreed a relative lift smaller than 10% wasn't worth three sprints of engineering time. Fourth, choose alpha and power: Chakor Mart's guidelines used the standard α = 0.05, two-sided, since the button could plausibly help or hurt, and power = 80%. Fifth — the step most teams skip or do only after the fact — calculate the required sample size from those four inputs and commit to running the test until that sample is reached, not until the dashboard looks good. Sixth, and only once that sample size is reached, look at the result exactly once and apply the rule agreed beforehand.

The step left most often implicit is the fourth-to-fifth handoff: treating MDE, alpha and power not as statistical trivia filled in by a data scientist but as a business conversation the PM and stakeholders have before the test starts, because each is a lever that changes how long the test must run and what it costs to learn the answer.

A worked example

Chakor Mart's data scientist, Rakesh Bhandari, used the standard two-proportion sample-size formula for equal-sized arms:

n (per arm) = (Zα/2 + Zβ)² × [p₁(1−p₁) + p₂(1−p₂)] / (p₂ − p₁)²

where p₁ is the baseline rate, p₂ the rate under the minimum detectable effect, Zα/2 is 1.96 for α = 0.05 two-sided, and Zβ is 0.84 for 80% power.

With p₁ = 0.040 and the agreed 10% relative MDE giving p₂ = 0.044: p₁(1−p₁) = 0.040 × 0.960 = 0.0384; p₂(1−p₂) = 0.044 × 0.956 = 0.04206; the two sum to 0.08046. The denominator (p₂ − p₁)² is 0.004² = 0.000016. The bracket (1.96 + 0.84)² is 2.80² = 7.84. So n = 7.84 × 0.08046 / 0.000016 ≈ 39,470 users per arm, roughly 79,000 across both arms. At 10,000 sessions per arm per day, that takes just under four days — yet Rakesh had scoped the test for sixteen, having built in margin for a more conservative second pass.

That second pass changes one input: what if 10% was too generous, and the business-relevant lift was really 5% relative (p₂ = 0.042)? With p₁(1−p₁) unchanged at 0.0384, p₂(1−p₂) = 0.042 × 0.958 = 0.04024, the sum is 0.07864, and (p₂ − p₁)² is 0.002² = 0.000004: n = 7.84 × 0.07864 / 0.000004 ≈ 154,050 per arm — about 308,000 in total, roughly sixteen days at Chakor Mart's traffic. Halving the effect size the test must detect nearly quadrupled the required sample, because the denominator is squared — the arithmetic reason "just detect a smaller effect" is rarely a free upgrade to a test's design.

The nuances a learner must sit with

Statistical significance is not practical significance. A large enough sample makes almost any tiny difference "significant" — Chakor Mart's own historical data show a rock-solid, operationally useless 0.3-point weekday-versus-weekend conversion gap. The minimum detectable effect exists to keep the test blind to effects too small to act on; choosing it too small is a common way to manufacture a headline nobody should build on.

Power protects against false negatives, and the two are easy to conflate. "Not significant" is routinely heard as "the feature doesn't work," when an underpowered test simply may not have had enough data to detect a real effect even if one existed. Silence from a weak test is not evidence of absence; it is evidence of not having looked hard enough.

Peeking does not just risk one wrong call; it changes the test's actual error rate. Checking a p-value daily and stopping the first time it dips below 0.05 can push the true chance of a false "win" well past the nominal 5% — sometimes above 20% — because each look is another roll of the dice on the same accumulating data, not an independent confirmation of the last one.

Novelty effects mean the true effect can drift across the test window, which looks like noise but is not. Users click a new button out of curiosity in week one; some of that lift fades by week three, or an initial dip from change-aversion recovers as users adjust. A test significant on day four has not ruled this out — only one held over several distinct weekly cohorts has.

The formula assumes independent observations, and that assumption quietly breaks. If the same customer checks out three times during the window, those sessions are correlated, not independent, which understates true variance and inflates how powered the test appears on paper.

"We have millions of users" confuses total scale with eligible sample. Chakor Mart has millions of app installs but only about 20,000 daily checkout sessions inside the funnel this test touches; the denominator that matters is almost always far smaller than the headline user count a company likes to quote.

A well-powered, significant test can still answer the wrong question. If the primary metric was chosen after scanning what moved rather than named in advance, the 0.05 threshold no longer means what it claims, because testing fifteen metrics raises the odds one turns green by chance alone — pre-registration is what keeps the number honest.

Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and company stage

The mechanics above hold everywhere, but what changes is how fast you reach the required sample. In a high-frequency consumer product like Chakor Mart, a well-powered test on a common flow can finish in days; the discipline problem is mostly resisting the urge to peek, since data arrives fast enough to make it tempting every few hours. In B2B products, the equivalent test — a new field on an admin console used by 200 enterprise accounts — may never reach a workable sample, because the unit of randomisation is often the account, not the user, and there simply aren't enough accounts; B2B teams typically substitute qualitative signals, such as structured feedback from account teams, or deliberately widen the MDE to match the traffic they actually have. Marketplace products add a further wrinkle: a change shown to sellers can affect what buyers see and vice versa, so independence breaks across the two sides of the market, usually requiring cluster-level randomisation by city or seller cohort rather than by session. Company stage matters too: an early-stage Chakor Mart, with a few thousand daily sessions, would have needed a much larger MDE — testing only changes expected to move conversion by 30–40%, not 5–10% — or months of runtime; a mature company with ten times the traffic can hunt for smaller effects in the same window, which is one reason "test everything" advice from large platforms travels badly to smaller ones.

Common mistakes

The first mistake is the one Meera nearly made: stopping early because the dashboard crossed the significance line. The symptom is a team shipping the moment a live p-value dips below 0.05, with relief rather than scrutiny. The misunderstanding is treating each daily look as a fresh, independent test rather than recognising that repeated looks share information and inflate the true error rate. The diagnostic: ask whether the test reached its pre-registered sample size before the decision, and if not, whether the team is using a sequential-testing method built for early stopping.

The second is declaring "no effect" from an underpowered test. The symptom is a confident "the redesign didn't move the needle," drawn from a week-long test on a low-traffic page. The misunderstanding is that a non-significant result proves the absence of an effect, when it may only prove the test lacked the sample to see one. The diagnostic: check what MDE the actual sample size could reliably have detected; if it is a 25% lift and the team hoped to catch a 5% one, the test never had a chance.

The third is metric shopping — reporting whichever of many tracked metrics turned significant. The symptom is a results deck leading with a metric nobody mentioned before launch. The diagnostic: check the pre-registration for which metric was named primary before day one, since testing fifteen metrics raises the odds one turns significant by chance alone.

The fourth is ignoring novelty decay — reading a strong week-one lift as the steady-state answer. The symptom is a rollout that "stops working" a month later. The diagnostic: plot the daily effect size, not just the cumulative one, and check whether it is flat or trending down.

What good looks like

Consider Rakesh's version of this same evening, two years earlier, testing a free-delivery threshold change. Before launch, the team wrote a one-page pre-registration: primary metric, baseline (3.7%), MDE (8% relative), alpha (0.05), power (80%), computed sample size (roughly 52,000 per arm), and planned duration (twelve days) — signed off by the PM, data scientist and engineering lead. The dashboard during the run showed only data-quality metrics, not a live p-value, so nobody could peek at significance and rationalise an early call. On day twelve, sample reached, the team looked once: an 11% lift, p = 0.018, holding steady through two further weeks run as a confirmation cohort before full rollout. The rollout decision took ten minutes, because the hard thinking had happened two weeks earlier, before anyone had seen a result.

Closing

Meera did not ask Arvind to wait until day sixteen out of caution for its own sake; she showed him Rakesh's original design — 39,470 per arm for the 10% MDE they had agreed mattered — and that by day five, with roughly 50,000 users per arm already in, they had in fact passed it, so this result deserved a green light. What she declined to do was treat the 0.041 as more solid than it was simply because it arrived early: had the test stopped at day three on an even better-looking 0.03, before reaching the required sample, the number would have been far less trustworthy. She sent Arvind the sample-size math, not just the result, and asked Rakesh to let the test run three more days as a confirmation window, watching for the novelty-decay pattern from the fourth mistake above. Her next topic to learn was sequential testing and always-valid inference — methods built for teams who need to look every day without paying the statistical price peeking normally exacts.

Two questions worth sitting with: if your last "significant" result had been checked only once, on a pre-committed date, would it still look significant? And what is the smallest lift your product would actually bother building for — have you written that number down before starting the test?

case20v1-exp.stats:
Ambar and the Green Dashboard

A teaching case on significance, power, sample size and stopping

1. Opening

At 9:30 a.m. on Friday, 23 October 2026, Inderpreet Pathania, head of product at Ambar, opened the experiment dashboard in the Gurugram office. The banner was green and read "Significant", as it had every morning since day four. The test, begun on Monday 12 October, split a random fifth of new users between the current home screen and one with a button, "Start with a popular basket". It was registered to run fourteen days, to Sunday 25 October. Today was day twelve, and eleven complete days of data were in.

Ambar's Diwali release had to be submitted to the app stores by 6 p.m. on Friday 23 October. Ikroop Pruthi, head of growth, wanted the button in that release for every new user. Ishnoor Panesar, the data scientist in Toronto, had written the test plan and wanted no decision before day fourteen. Inderpreet had until evening to choose.

2. Company background

Ambar was founded in Ludhiana in 2019 by two former kirana distributors who noticed that grocery apps built for Bengaluru and Mumbai assumed a delivery density, basket size and payment habit that Punjab, Haryana, Himachal and Jammu did not share. The app delivers staples, dairy, produce and festival goods within two to four hours, and most orders are paid by UPI. In the year to March 2026 it sold goods worth ₹640 crore. Ambar employs 410 people, with product and engineering in Gurugram and Pune and a small analytics team in Toronto.

Its rivals are larger: Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart, now present in most tier-two cities, BigBasket and JioMart behind the Tata and Reliance networks, and Flipkart Minutes. Ambar competes on regional assortment, from sarson and makki flour to Amul ghee at festival prices. It receives about 10,700 new installs a day in an ordinary week, around 15,000 a day in the Diwali fortnight, and most are bought through paid advertising.

3. The situation

In the control version of the app, about 70 per cent of new users left their first session without ordering. The button offered a pre-filled starter basket of the ten items most often bought first in the user's city. The design lead in Berlin, who is three and a half hours behind Gurugram until 25 October, drew it in September, and engineers in Pune built it behind a remote flag, so any group of users can be switched on or off without a new release.

Ishnoor registered the plan on 9 October (Exhibit 1). Assignment uses a hashed device identifier, so the test collects nothing beyond what Ambar's notice under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 already covers. The single metric was whether a new user ordered within twenty-four hours of first opening the app. Baseline was 30 per cent, and the smallest gain worth shipping was 1.5 percentage points. Ambar enrols 20 per cent of installs, 2,140 a day, split evenly. Fourteen days gives 14,980 users per arm. The plan specified one reading, on day fourteen.

The dashboard, however, refreshes every morning. Exhibit 2 shows what it displayed. Through day three the p-value was 0.0492 and the banner turned green the next morning; through day eleven the lift was 1.33 points and p was 0.0275. Ikroop pointed to the last row of the cumulative table. Ishnoor, who sees the same numbers at midnight in Toronto, pointed to the three blocks beneath it and to the figure.

The calendar adds pressure (Exhibit 3 gives the money). Dhanteras falls on 6 November and Diwali on 8 November. Finance values each extra first-day buyer at ₹1,200 of ninety-day contribution, and the home-screen shelf the button would displace for new users, "Festive hamper", is forecast to earn ₹14 lakh over the fortnight.

4. The people

Ikroop Pruthi, head of growth, Gurugram. She has spent nine years in consumer apps and has the Diwali creative, built around the button, waiting for approval. "Eleven days is more than most tests get," she says. "The banner has been green for nine mornings, and Diwali does not move for us." She also controls the paid-install budget, and wants the button live before the heaviest spending begins on 27 October.

Ishnoor Panesar, senior data scientist, Toronto. Nine and a half hours behind Gurugram until 1 November, she wrote the plan and its sample-size calculation. She wants the registered reading honoured, and would like the decision rule written down before the numbers arrive.

Ivneet Pahuja, engineering manager, Pune. His team must cut the release build by Friday evening. He needs to know whether the button ships on, ships off behind the flag, or is removed. Any of the three costs him the same effort, provided the instruction does not change on Saturday.

5. Exhibits

6. The options

Option A: stop today and ship. Submit Friday's build with the button on for all new users from Saturday 24 October. The Diwali creative can be approved at once, and about 29,000 more new users see the button over 24–26 October. The test closes at 11,770 users per arm, and no further reading is taken.

Option B: finish the registered test. Submit the build with the button flagged off for everyone outside the test. Take the single reading on Monday 26 October at 14,980 users per arm, and switch the flag on from Tuesday 27 October if the result warrants. About 29,000 new users miss three days of the button, and the creative waits until Monday.

Option C: extend the test. Keep the 20 per cent split to Saturday 7 November, 33,275 users per arm, enough to detect a 1.0-point gain with 80 per cent power. Ninety per cent of Diwali-fortnight new users never see the button.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What did the registered plan promise, and what can and cannot be concluded from eleven days of data?
  2. The banner has been green since day three. What claim does a green banner make, and how much weight should p = 0.0275 carry?
  3. What do the three blocks in Exhibit 2 suggest, what would you need to see before calling it real, and where does Exhibit 3 put the line between shipping and not shipping?
  4. Which option would you take on 23 October, what decision rule would you write down before Monday, and what result would change your mind?

8. A note for the learner

Significance, power and sample size are three promises made before the data arrive: how often a null effect may be mistaken for a win, how likely a real effect of a stated size is to be found, and how many users that takes. Peeking weakens the first promise. A decision rule that reacts to each morning's number is a different test from the one registered, and early estimates also tend to run high when users are new to a feature.

One defensible path is Option B with a rule fixed on Thursday. Submit the build flagged off. On Monday, ship if the fourteen-day result is significant at 0.05. At 14,980 per arm that needs a lift near 1.0 point, so significance binds, and the 0.56-point break-even (₹14 lakh ÷ 2,10,000 users ÷ ₹1,200) is the commercial floor beneath it. Otherwise keep the shelf and rerun the button after Diwali at the size Exhibit 1 gives for 1.0 point. The cost is three days of exposure; the gain is a number that means what it says.

ISB · Software Product Management · Case

Beeja Systems: Six Days in November

Bengaluru · Pune · Berlin · Toronto · Singapore · New Jersey · Dubai

1. Sunday night, Bengaluru

At a quarter past eleven on the night of Sunday, 22 November 2026, Jaspreet Rangi sat on the floor of her flat off Bannerghatta Road, four printouts fanned across the rug. The board of Beeja Systems meets at ten, and the only item that mattered was whether to sign the Bariq Retail Group pilot as Bariq's procurement had sent it back, uplift guarantee intact.

The reconciliation on top answered one question five ways: how much money the nudge Beeja shipped to Bilori Fashion on 8 November was making. One row said eighteen per cent, one two point two, one one point seven; two could not rule out zero. All five came from Beeja's own logs, and Jaspreet had signed the client report quoting the first.

What she had to settle before ten o'clock was what to say about clause 9.3, and in what order.

2. Beeja Systems, 2019–2026

Beeja Systems was founded in Bengaluru in 2019 by Jatinder Ranhotra and two colleagues from an analytics consultancy. Its product is an SDK inside a consumer app or retail checkout that decides which nudge a shopper sees — a basket suggestion, a reorder prompt, a delivery-slot choice — and measures what it did. By October 2026 it had twenty-eight paying clients, eighty-six employees (forty-one in Bengaluru, twenty-four in Pune, five in Singapore, six in New Jersey, three in Toronto, two in Berlin, two in Dubai, three elsewhere) and FY26 contracted fees of ₹18.20 crore (Exhibit 4) against ₹12.60 crore in FY25.

One decision from 2022 shaped everything after it. Competitors sold measurement as a report that arrived after a test ended; Jatinder sold the opposite. In March 2022 Beeja shipped Live Lift, a console panel showing a client its measured lift and a confidence readout that refreshed on every page load. From the third standard agreement onwards it was a contractual deliverable, not a feature — "continuous visibility of measured uplift and statistical confidence" — and in March 2024 Beeja tied a quarter of Bilori's annual fee to a measured attach-rate uplift. Both still bind: Beeja cannot withdraw the panel without amending a client's agreement, or amend Bilori's before the March audit without reopening the fee.

3. The market

The category is crowded. VWO out of Delhi, CleverTap, MoEngage and WebEngage sell experimentation or engagement tooling to Indian consumer businesses; Optimizely and Adobe Target hold the enterprise end; Statsig and GrowthBook have pulled the mid-market towards cheaper developer-run testing. When Google retired Optimize in 2023, mid-market buyers had to pay for a tool for the first time, and Beeja won eleven clients in the eighteen months after. At the top the question does not arise: Flipkart, Meesho, Nykaa, Zepto and Swiggy build their own.

Two forces press on the product. The DPDP Act's consent requirements make a cross-app identity graph expensive, so user-level measurement in India covers logged-in sessions only; and ONDC is pulling checkout traffic into flows Beeja does not own. Abroad, Beeja has a Gulf business built on three retail groups, of which Bariq is the largest, and a New Jersey pipeline that has not closed a logo. Bariq's session data sits in a UAE region under local rules and does not leave it; Toronto sees daily aggregates and in-region summaries, nothing finer.

4. What happened, and what was believed

Bariq signed a memorandum of understanding on 14 September 2026: a thirty-day pilot at ₹90 lakh, convertible on success into a three-year licence at ₹7.50 crore a year. Success sits in clause 9.3 — "an uplift in net revenue per session of not less than two per cent, demonstrated at ninety-five per cent confidence". Jashan Raikhy negotiated it: procurement asked for the confidence language and he agreed on the strength of the +5.1 per cent in Beeja's Gulf deck for Bariq's own carousel test, row T-16 of Exhibit 1.

The flagship test that autumn was elsewhere. On Tuesday 3 November, Jaival Ranauta's redesigned basket nudge went live on Bilori's checkout as T-31, split evenly across all eligible sessions, planned for fourteen days. The panel showed a rising attach rate from the first morning, and on day three the confidence readout crossed ninety-five per cent and stayed there. On the evening of Sunday 8 November, Diwali, with the festival peak still running, Bilori asked for full exposure. Beeja agreed: the test stopped at the end of day six, treatment went to ninety per cent of sessions, ten per cent held back. Jaspreet's report of 9 November led with the attach-rate figure; Exhibit 3 plots what the panel had shown.

Three things have since come to light. On 12 November Jaival mentioned in a product channel that he had pushed a second change into the same arm on day two: a price anchor by the suggested item, shipped as copy polish. On 16 November the holdback read for days seven to fourteen came back at +0.60 per cent on revenue per session, its interval containing zero. On 17 November Jivesh Raina circulated Exhibit 5, the same test computed five ways, with Exhibit 2, which gives each client's days of traffic needed to detect the effect 9.3 guarantees. Figure 1 sets out the sequence.

Figure 1 — November 2026, from Beeja's release and reporting logs

Ticks mark the start of the named date; the axis runs 1 to 30 November 2026. The boxes above are earlier decisions, not to scale. Diwali fell on Sunday 8 November 2026.

5. The people

Jaspreet Rangi, VP Product, Bengaluru. Holds that Beeja should not sign 9.3 as drafted and should write a decision rule into the pilot. Product owns the Live Lift roadmap; she approved the report quoting eighteen per cent to Bilori, and has not told the board she read Exhibit 2 on 17 November and said nothing on Thursday's forecast call.

Jatinder Ranhotra, co-founder and CEO, Bengaluru, wants the pilot signed this month: a ₹140 crore Series B is in discussion against a run-rate milestone of ₹25 crore, and he adds Bariq's ₹7.50 crore a year to ₹18.20 crore to reach ₹25.70 crore annualised, a base that includes the one-off ₹90 lakh pilot fee. He is not saying he has described the Gulf licence to the lead investor as agreed.

Jagruti Rehsi, Director of Engineering, Pune, owns the panel. Holds that it reports what it always has and that no client would accept a slower console; her bonus is tied to shipped features. She has not circulated ticket BEE-2214, filed July 2024, which recorded that the panel recomputes a fixed-horizon confidence figure on every page load, uncorrected for the number of looks.

Jivesh Raina, Senior Data Scientist, Toronto, wrote Exhibits 2 and 5. Holds that Beeja should adopt an always-valid sequential boundary and restate Exhibit 1 under it; he filed BEE-2214 and has argued it for three quarters. He is not saying that he is interviewing elsewhere, nor that he chose to pool rows one and two after seeing row two.

Jashan Raikhy, Head of Sales, North America and Gulf, New Jersey, wants the signature; forty per cent of his pay is variable on booked contract value and Bariq is his quarter. He is not saying that he accepted the ninety-five per cent wording without Legal, because procurement would not reopen commercial terms if the clause were touched.

Janvika Ramgarhia, Head of Customer Success, Singapore, runs the Gulf accounts. Holds that the clause should be reworded to a metric Beeja can report inside thirty days, and that Bariq will accept this if asked early; her bonus is net revenue retention. She has not told Jaspreet that in October she assured procurement the pilot "will read at thirty days".

Jaival Ranauta, Principal Designer, Berlin, designed the nudge. Holds that the effect is real and the decline across the holdback is shopper fatigue, not measurement error: someone who has seen the nudge twenty times stops noticing it. His stake is the design system's standing. He has disclosed the day-two anchor but does not accept that it makes the arm two changes.

8. The options as Jaspreet sees them

A. Sign clause 9.3 as drafted. The pilot starts 1 December at full exposure, reporting on the panel on 30 December. It books the ₹90 lakh pilot fee, keeps the licence at ₹7.50 crore a year inside the Series B window, and puts the whole ₹90 lakh under the waiver. It leaves the panel, Exhibit 1's eight results and the reports already sent to clients as they are.

B. Ask Bariq for a ninety-day window and a written decision rule. One analysis at a stated horizon, with the metric and the test named in the contract. It moves the report past the 20 January review and out of Jashan's quarter, and defers the ₹90 lakh and the licence. It leaves Bilori's clause and the March audit untouched.

C. Move every client to an always-valid sequential boundary. The panel would show a bound that holds however often it is read, and Exhibit 1's eight tests would be restated under it. Jagruti costs it at twenty-two engineer-weeks, or ₹34 lakh at Beeja's loaded Pune rate of ₹1.55 lakh an engineer-week, against a committed roadmap. It reopens Bilori's attach-rate calculation and the ₹1.05 crore the March audit tests. On Bariq it reaches only the aggregates that leave the UAE region.

D. Rewrite clause 9.3 onto attach rate. Attach rate is the metric Bilori's own clause is written on, and it keeps the thirty-day window and the 1 December start. It asks procurement to accept a metric that is not in their category review, and Janvika to go back on what she said in October. It leaves the revenue-per-session question where it is.
